title: Freeze the Value You Have, Pass On the Growth You Will Make
summary: An estate freeze fixes the value of what a person owns today and lets future growth build up in the hands of the next generation, often through a trust. It does not remove tax; it decides whose balance sheet the growth lands on. Learn the mechanics in plain words before any adviser shows you a share diagram.
body:
An estate freeze does one thing: it caps the value of what you own today at today's number, so that every dollar of growth after that belongs to someone else, usually your children or a trust for them. It moves future growth, not past growth, and it moves tax with it.

Recall

Q. What is a letter of wishes?

A. A non-binding note from a settlor explaining what she hopes trustees will consider when they exercise discretion. It guides; it does not bind.

Q. In asset protection, why does a transfer made before any claim stand better than one made after?

A. Because a transfer made in calm water, for real purposes, looks like planning, while one made once a claim is in view looks like an attempt to defeat a creditor, which voidable transfer rules exist to reverse.

Q. What is a red team review?

A. An independent group asked to attack a plan, structure or estimate as an opponent would, to find weaknesses before a lender, auditor or market does.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a successful developer's main asset is usually a private company whose value grows with every project. If nothing is done, that growth piles up in the founder's own name until death, when it may meet tax, probate and family disputes all at once. An estate freeze is one of the oldest tools for deciding, in advance and on purpose, where that growth goes. Elias joins me because a freeze is as much a tax event as a family one. Everything here is concept teaching. Freeze mechanics and their tax results vary by jurisdiction and change over time, and nothing here is a conclusion about any particular place. Professional sign-off required: a tax lawyer or tax accountant, and a trust lawyer, in the relevant jurisdiction.

The mechanics in plain words

Picture a hypothetical holding company worth 10,000,000 dollars today, owned entirely by its founder through ordinary shares. In a typical freeze, three things happen.

  1. The founder exchanges his ordinary shares for freeze shares: fixed-value shares, usually preferred, that are redeemable for exactly 10,000,000 dollars and carry a fixed dividend entitlement, if any, but no right to future growth.
  2. New growth shares, ordinary shares that carry all value above the frozen amount, are issued for a nominal price to the next generation or, more often, to a family trust.
  3. From that day, if the company grows to 25,000,000 dollars, the founder's shares are still worth 10,000,000 dollars, and the 15,000,000 dollars of growth sits with the growth shares.

The founder can often keep control through voting rights attached to his freeze shares, depending on how they are designed and what local law permits. That is why freezes appeal to developers: the founder keeps running the company while the future value leaves his estate.

Say that out loud now.

The professional framing

Three questions decide whether a freeze works. First, is the frozen value right? If the founder exchanges shares worth 10,000,000 dollars for freeze shares redeemable at 8,000,000 dollars, he has quietly given 2,000,000 dollars to the growth shareholders, which a tax authority may treat as a taxable benefit or gift. Freezes therefore rely on an independent valuation and often a price adjustment clause: a term that automatically corrects the redemption amount if a tax authority or court later finds the value was different. Second, do the freeze shares really hold their value? If they can be stripped by excessive dividends to the growth shares, or diluted, they are not truly fixed. Third, who holds the growth shares, and on what terms? A family trust gives flexibility about which family member eventually benefits, but brings in all the trustee duties and tax rules of the last two weeks.

Applied example, hypothetical. A founder freezes at 10,000,000 dollars and a discretionary trust for his three children subscribes for growth shares at 100 dollars. Over 15 years the company grows to 24,000,000 dollars. The founder's estate holds 10,000,000 dollars of freeze shares. The trust holds about 14,000,000 dollars of value. Whatever tax applies to the founder at death is computed on the frozen value, not the full 24,000,000 dollars, subject to local rules. The growth has not escaped tax. It has moved to a different taxpayer, with a different timetable.

What a freeze cannot do

A freeze does not erase gains that already exist on the frozen value. The 10,000,000 dollars, less whatever the founder paid for his shares, remains a latent gain in his hands. A freeze does not cancel tax on the growth either; it shifts that tax onto the growth shareholders and their own events, including, in some systems, periodic tax events inside trusts. And a freeze cannot be undone cheaply. Once growth shares are issued to a trust, that value belongs to the trust and its beneficiaries. A founder who later regrets it, after a divorce in the family, for example, cannot simply take it back.

A second applied example, hypothetical. A founder freezes, then keeps paying himself large dividends on the freeze shares to fund his lifestyle. If those dividends reduce the company's value below what the freeze shares can be redeemed for, or if they are paid in ways the share terms do not allow, the structure starts to fail on its own terms. If he instead pays dividends to the growth shares held by the trust and the trust then distributes to his young children, attribution rules in some systems may tax that income back to him. We take attribution apart on Day 4.

Timing

The best time to freeze is before the growth, which is to say when the company is small and the future is uncertain. That is also when founders least want to think about it. A freeze done at 2,000,000 dollars of value moves far more future growth than one done at 20,000,000 dollars. The cost of waiting is invisible each year and very large over a career.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a freeze built on a soft valuation. If the frozen value is too low, the founder may have made an unintended taxable gift; if it is too high, the freeze shares carry phantom value the company cannot support. The control is an independent valuation by a qualified business valuator, a price adjustment clause where local law gives it effect, and a file that records the method and evidence used.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is thinking a freeze is a way to keep everything while giving nothing. The founder keeps today's value and, often, control. He genuinely gives away the future. If he is not ready to do that, he is not ready to freeze.

Callback

Two lessons ago, Warrick showed that assets put into a trust leave your personal balance sheet. A freeze does the same thing to future value: your net worth stops growing with the company, and your lender will see that. Plan your liquidity and guarantee capacity on the frozen number, not the company's growth.

Six-Lens Check

Tax. A freeze relocates future gains and may be a taxable event if mispriced; local rules decide. Liability. Directors and trustees each carry duties around redemptions and dividends. Banking. Lenders will re-examine who owns and controls the borrower after a share reorganisation. Governance. Voting rights, redemption terms and dividend policy must be written into the share terms and a shareholders' agreement. Estate. The founder's estate is capped at the frozen value, subject to local rules. Exit. On a sale, the freeze shares take their fixed amount and the growth shares take the rest, so model a sale before you freeze.

Recap

A freeze caps today's value in fixed-value shares and sends future growth to growth shares, often held by a trust. It needs an honest valuation, real fixed terms and a ready founder. It moves tax; it does not delete it.

Next lesson: Ford, with Cole assisting, on a frozen family business whose offshore trust was found to live in Canada.
checklist: I can explain freeze shares and growth shares in one sentence each.
I insist on an independent valuation by a qualified business valuator before any freeze.
I ask whether a price adjustment clause is available and effective locally.
I check that the freeze shares cannot be stripped or diluted.
I decide who holds the growth shares and on what terms before the reorganisation.
I model a sale of the company before and after the freeze.
I plan my liquidity and guarantee capacity on the frozen value.
I get tax and trust sign-off in the relevant jurisdiction before signing.
head: Field checklist
speak: An estate freeze caps the value of what you own today and sends future growth to someone else. Hypothetically, a founder owns a company worth 10,000,000 dollars. He exchanges his ordinary shares for fixed-value freeze shares redeemable at 10,000,000 dollars, and new growth shares are issued for a nominal sum, often to a family trust. If the company later reaches 24,000,000 dollars, his shares are still worth 10,000,000 and the trust holds the growth. He may keep control through voting rights. Three questions decide whether it works: is the frozen value right, backed by an independent valuation and often a price adjustment clause; are the freeze shares truly fixed; and who holds the growth, on what terms. A freeze does not erase existing gains, does not cancel tax on growth, and cannot be cheaply undone. It moves tax to another taxpayer. Professional sign-off is required in the relevant jurisdiction.
terms: Estate freeze — a reorganisation that fixes the value of a person's current holding and lets future growth accrue to others.
Freeze shares — fixed-value shares, usually preferred and redeemable, that carry today's value but no right to future growth.
Price adjustment clause — a term that automatically corrects a share's redemption amount if its value is later found to be different.

hostile.q: You did an estate freeze last year and your children's trust now owns the growth shares. Why should I treat you as the controlling party for this loan?
hostile.a: Because I still hold all the voting shares, and the share terms and shareholders' agreement say so. I will give you the share terms, the register and the trust deed. Economically, my own stake is capped at the frozen value, and my personal statement shows that figure, not the company's full value. If you need the trust to support the loan, that is a decision for its independent trustees, and they will take their own advice.

title: Fundy Settlement: The Offshore Trust That Lived at Home
summary: A Canadian family's estate freeze put growth shares into trusts with a trustee in Barbados, and a large gain on sale was claimed to be exempt under a tax treaty. Canada's Supreme Court held in 2012 that the trusts were resident in Canada because that is where the real decisions were made. Seven forensic steps show why substance beat the trustee's address.
body:
A trust lives where its real decisions are made, not where its trustee's office is. In the Fundy Settlement case, Canada's Supreme Court held in 2012 that trusts with a Barbados trustee were resident in Canada, and the treaty plan built on that address collapsed.

Recall

Q. What duty does a trustee breach by lending trust money to his own company?

A. The duty of loyalty, which forbids putting personal interest in conflict with duty and dealing with trust property for oneself without authorisation. Rule 90 came from it.

Q. What is the difference between ring-fencing and hiding assets?

A. Ring-fencing separates risks openly and in advance for business reasons. Hiding assets moves them to defeat a creditor, which voidable transfer rules can reverse.

Q. Why should you critique your own advisers?

A. Because advisers can be wrong, conflicted or out of date, and you carry the consequences. Asking for their reasoning, assumptions and risks in writing is part of using them well.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this case joins this week's two subjects: an estate freeze, which sent future growth to trusts, and the question of where a trust is taxed. It is a real case. I give only the facts I am confident of, and I leave out figures; read the judgment itself before relying on any detail. Cole assists because the failure is one of evidence: the paperwork said one thing, and the conduct said another.

1. Timeline

In the late 1990s, as part of a reorganisation of family holding companies in Ontario that worked as an estate freeze, growth shares were acquired by two trusts, each settled with a trustee resident in Barbados. Some years later the family's business interests were sold and the trusts realised a large capital gain. The trusts took the position that they were resident in Barbados and that the Canada-Barbados tax treaty exempted the gain from Canadian tax. The Canada Revenue Agency assessed the trusts as resident in Canada. The Tax Court of Canada agreed with the tax authority in 2009, the Federal Court of Appeal upheld that in 2010, and the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed the trusts' appeal in 2012. Verify the dates against the judgments before you rely on them.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Choosing an offshore trust company as trustee to place the trusts' residence in a treaty country. Structuring the sale so that the gain arose in the trusts. And, crucially, continuing to have the substantive decisions about the trusts' assets made by the family and its advisers in Canada, while the Barbados trustee carried out administrative functions.

3. Assumptions

The central assumption was that a trust is resident where its trustee resides. That had long been a widely held working view. The Supreme Court held instead that the residence of a trust, like that of a corporation, is generally found where its central management and control actually takes place. The trial findings were that this happened in Canada, with the Barbados trustee playing a limited role. A secondary assumption was that a treaty would protect the gain once residence was established; with residence lost, the treaty claim fell away.

4. Incentives

The incentive was obvious and lawful in itself: the gain was large, and a treaty exemption, if available, would have saved substantial tax. The trustee's incentive was to provide a service for a fee. The family's incentive was to keep decisions about its own wealth close to home. Those last two incentives pointed in opposite directions from the structure's needs, which required the trustee, not the family, to decide.

Say that out loud now.

5. Warning signs ignored

Cole lists the signs an auditor would have flagged. The trustee was a service provider with limited involvement in substantive investment decisions. Key decisions appear to have been taken by people in Canada. The structure's tax result depended entirely on one fact, residence, while the conduct undermined that fact. Whenever a structure's value rests on where decisions are made, and decision-makers keep acting somewhere else, the structure is weaker than its documents look.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the period in which decisions about the trusts' assets, and the sale in particular, were made without genuine trustee judgment exercised in Barbados. Once those decisions had been made that way, the evidence existed, and no later paperwork could change where control had in fact been exercised.

7. Root cause

The root cause was confusing a trust's address with its substance. A trustee is not a mailbox. If the trustee does not genuinely make the decisions, a tax authority and a court may look for whoever does, and tax the trust where they sit. The same root cause appeared in our residence and substance week: mind and management follow the people who decide.

What a trustee who really decides looks like

A worked illustration, hypothetical, of the evidence a genuinely managed trust would hold. The trustee meets in its own jurisdiction four times a year. Before each meeting it receives a board pack prepared for it, not by it after the fact. It obtains its own investment and legal advice. It sometimes declines a family request, and the minutes record why. It signs sale documents only after its own review, with time to do it. Each of those items is evidence of central management and control in the trustee's jurisdiction. In a structure where the trustee merely signs what arrives, none of them exists.

A second worked illustration, hypothetical, of what the stakes look like on paper. Suppose a trust realises a gain of 50,000,000 dollars, and suppose, purely hypothetically, that an effective tax rate of 25 percent would apply if it is resident at home. The tax at stake is 12,500,000 dollars, before interest. A structure whose entire value is a number of that size, resting on a single disputable fact, deserves the most careful evidence-keeping in the family's affairs. Rates and outcomes depend on the jurisdiction and the facts; verify against the primary source.

Cole's evidence test

Cole applies one test to any structure whose result depends on where decisions are made. Take the last three major decisions and ask, for each: who first proposed it, who analysed it, who could have said no, and where were they when they said yes? Hypothetically, suppose the answers for a family trust are that the founder's accountant proposed a sale, the founder's lawyer analysed it, the founder could have said no, and the offshore trustee signed the documents two days after they arrived by courier. The paper trail then points straight at the founder's home jurisdiction, whatever the deed says. Run the same test on a healthy structure and the answers name the trustee at every step, in its own jurisdiction, with time and advice to decide. The test takes an hour. It is worth running every year, and before any large transaction, because the evidence it examines is created continuously and cannot be recreated later.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a structure whose tax result depends on where decisions are made, run by people who make them somewhere else. The control is a governance calendar and evidence file in the trustee's jurisdiction, genuine trustee advice and judgment, and a standing rule that no family member or adviser makes or pre-agrees trust decisions.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is treating a structure's legal documents as its whole existence. Documents describe; conduct decides. Professional sign-off required: a tax lawyer and a trust lawyer in each relevant jurisdiction.

Callback

In the substance week, Elias and I said that residence follows the people who actually decide, and that a substance record must be kept as it happens. Fundy Settlement is the trust version of that lesson, and it reached the highest court in the country.

Recap

An estate freeze sent growth to trusts with an offshore trustee. A large gain on sale was claimed exempt under a treaty. The Supreme Court of Canada held in 2012 that the trusts were resident where central management and control was exercised, in Canada.

Rule 91: Never rest a structure's tax result on a trustee's or director's address; it lives where real decisions are made, so make them there, by the people entitled to make them, and keep the evidence as you go.

Next lesson: Warrick, on what a freeze moves on a family's balance sheet.
checklist: I identify every structure whose tax result depends on where decisions are made.
I confirm trustees and directors genuinely decide, with their own advice.
I keep board packs, minutes and advice in the decision-maker's jurisdiction.
I never let family members or advisers pre-agree trust decisions.
I treat a passive service-provider trustee as a warning sign.
I read the actual judgments before relying on any tax case.
I get tax and trust sign-off in each relevant jurisdiction before a sale.
head: Field checklist
speak: Fundy Settlement is a real Canadian case. As part of a family business reorganisation that worked as an estate freeze, growth shares went into trusts with a trustee in Barbados. When the business interests were later sold, the trusts claimed a large gain was exempt under the Canada-Barbados treaty because the trusts were resident in Barbados. The Tax Court in 2009, the Federal Court of Appeal in 2010 and the Supreme Court of Canada in 2012 held otherwise: a trust's residence is generally where its central management and control actually takes place, and that was found to be in Canada, with the Barbados trustee playing a limited role. The root cause was confusing a trust's address with its substance. Documents describe; conduct decides. Rule 91: never rest a structure's tax result on an address; it lives where real decisions are made, so make them there and keep the evidence. Read the judgments before relying on any detail.
terms: Central management and control — the test of where the highest-level decisions of an entity are actually made, used to find residence.
Trust residence — the jurisdiction in which a trust is treated as living for tax purposes, which decides where it is taxed.
Treaty exemption — relief under a tax treaty that removes or reduces tax in one country on income or gains, available only to a qualifying resident.

hostile.q: Your family trust has a foreign trustee, and you are telling me its gain is not taxable here. Show me who actually decided to sell.
hostile.a: The trustee decided, in its own jurisdiction, and the file shows it: the board pack it received, the independent valuation and legal advice it obtained, the meeting minutes recording its deliberation, and the fact that it negotiated two terms the family had not asked for. Our tax advisers have reviewed the residence position in writing. If any decision was made elsewhere, I would rather we find it now than defend it later.

rule: Rule 91: Never rest a structure's tax result on a trustee's or director's address; it lives where real decisions are made, so make them there, by the people entitled to make them, and keep the evidence as you go.

title: What a Freeze Moves on the Family Balance Sheet
summary: A freeze changes nothing about the company's value and everything about who owns its growth. Measured over a generation, the shift can be very large, along with the deferral of tax and the loss of the founder's personal flexibility. This lesson puts round numbers on both sides.
body:
A freeze does not make the family richer on the day it is signed. It changes who will be rich later, and when tax will be due, and those two changes compound for decades.

Recall

Q. What are freeze shares and growth shares?

A. Freeze shares are fixed-value, usually preferred, shares that carry today's value but no future growth. Growth shares carry all value above the frozen amount.

Q. What does personal leverage do to a wealth builder's risk?

A. It magnifies both gains and losses on personal equity and can force sales at the worst time, which is why position sizing and liquidity tiers matter.

Q. What is a structure audit?

A. An independent review that tests whether a legal and tax structure works as designed, with the evidence its results depend on actually in place.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a freeze is often presented in one diagram and one sentence: "future growth goes to the trust, tax saved". The real effects run across three balance sheets: yours, the trust's and the company's. They also run across time. If you can put numbers on those effects, you can judge a freeze proposal on its merits. All numbers here are hypothetical and round. Tax rates are placeholders, not facts, and a licensed adviser is required before you act.

The growth that moves

Plain English: the money that moves is the company's future growth. The professional framing is value shift: the transfer, over time, of economic value from the founder's shares to the growth shares, measured as the company's future value minus the frozen amount.

Worked example, hypothetical. A holding company is worth 8,000,000 dollars when the founder freezes. It grows at 7 percent a year. After 10 years, 1.07 raised to the 10th power is about 1.967, so the company is worth about 15,740,000 dollars. The founder's freeze shares are worth 8,000,000 dollars. The growth shares are worth about 7,740,000 dollars. After 20 years, the factor is about 3.870, the company is worth about 30,960,000 dollars, and the growth shares hold about 22,960,000 dollars. In 20 years almost three quarters of the company's value has moved off the founder's balance sheet, without a single further transfer.

Say that out loud now.

The tax that moves with it

Suppose, hypothetically, that the founder's jurisdiction taxes accrued gains when a person dies, as some systems do through a deemed disposition, and suppose a placeholder effective rate of 25 percent on the gain. Suppose his cost base in the shares is 500,000 dollars.

Without a freeze, if he dies in year 20, his gain is about 30,960,000 minus 500,000, roughly 30,460,000 dollars. At the placeholder rate, tax is about 7,615,000 dollars. With a freeze, his gain at death is 8,000,000 minus 500,000, which is 7,500,000 dollars, and tax is about 1,875,000 dollars. The difference, about 5,740,000 dollars, is not tax saved forever. The growth shares carry their own latent gain of about 22,960,000 dollars, which will meet tax on their holders' own events, which may include periodic deemed dispositions inside a trust in some systems. What the freeze buys is a change of taxpayer and, often, a long deferral. Deferral has real value: a liability due in 30 years costs far less in today's money than one due in 20.

What the founder gives up

Now the other side. The founder's personal wealth stops growing with the company. If he lives 25 more years and the company prospers, he holds a fixed 8,000,000 dollars while the family's total grows past 30,000,000 dollars. If he later needs cash, he redeems freeze shares, which reduces his stake and may itself be taxed. If the company falls in value below 8,000,000 dollars, the freeze shares absorb the loss first, and the growth shares are worthless. The freeze moves the upside; the downside largely stays with the founder.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Ten years after the freeze, the founder wants 2,000,000 dollars for a new venture of his own. The company redeems 2,000,000 dollars of his freeze shares. His stake drops to 6,000,000 dollars. The redemption may be treated as a dividend or a disposition, depending on local rules, and taxed accordingly. A founder who freezes too early, or freezes everything, can find himself asset-rich in a company whose growth belongs to others and short of personal liquidity. Many advisers suggest a partial freeze or keeping some growth shares personally for exactly this reason; that is a planning choice, not a rule.

How the best do it

Well-run family enterprises treat a freeze as one step in a written plan rather than a one-off transaction. The common practice is to model the founder's lifetime cash needs first, freeze only what exceeds them, obtain an independent valuation with documented assumptions, and revisit the structure at defined intervals, sometimes with a refreeze if value has fallen. A small developer can copy the order of operations: personal needs first, then the freeze, then the review calendar.

Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet after a freeze, the line for company shares becomes a fixed number. Your net worth growth now depends on your other assets and your income. Your estate's potential tax liability is capped on the frozen value, subject to local rules, and should be shown as a contingent liability at that figure. Your lender's view of your guarantee strength will freeze too, so plan any future personal guarantees on the frozen value.

What it does to the family's balance sheet

Step back and draw the family as a single balance sheet, because that is how the next generation will experience it. Hypothetically, on the 20-year numbers, the family owns a company worth about 30,960,000 dollars either way. Without a freeze, the whole value and a tax liability of about 7,615,000 dollars sit in one person's estate, all crystallising on one unknown date. With a freeze, about 8,000,000 dollars and a liability of about 1,875,000 dollars sit in the estate, and about 22,960,000 dollars sit in the trust with a latent liability of its own, falling due on events the trustees can plan around. The family's total wealth before tax is identical. What changes is concentration of timing: instead of one large tax event on a date nobody chooses, the family has two smaller ones, at least one of which it can schedule. For a family whose main asset is an illiquid private company, that difference can decide whether a property must be sold in a bad market to pay a bill. Put both versions of the family balance sheet side by side in front of the founder, with the dates of each tax event marked, and the conversation about whether to freeze becomes a conversation about timing and control rather than about a headline saving.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is freezing so much that the founder cannot fund his own life without redemptions that cost tax and control. The control is a written lifetime cash-needs model, built before the freeze, that leaves the founder enough personal liquidity and income on conservative assumptions.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is presenting the tax difference at death as money saved. It is mostly tax moved and deferred. Present it that way to your family and your advisers, or you will make decisions on a number that is not real.

Callback

In the capital allocation week, Roman and I treated concentration as a deliberate risk to size and record. A freeze leaves the founder concentrated in a fixed-value claim on one company, while the family is concentrated in its growth. Both concentrations need to be visible on the family's one-page wealth map.

Recap

A freeze shifts future value from the founder to the growth shareholders, and with it the latent tax. Over 20 years that shift can be most of the company. The founder keeps the downside and loses the upside, so his own cash needs come first.

Next lesson: Elias, on the rules: attribution, deemed disposition and two systems compared.
checklist: I model the company's value at the freeze and at 10 and 20 years on stated growth rates.
I show the value shift to growth shareholders in dollars.
I present tax effects as moved and deferred, not saved.
I build a lifetime cash-needs model for the founder before freezing.
I consider a partial freeze or keeping some growth shares personally.
I show the capped estate tax exposure as a contingent liability on my balance sheet.
I plan future guarantees on the frozen value.
I set a review calendar, including whether a refreeze makes sense.
head: Field checklist
speak: A freeze does not make a family richer on day one; it changes who gets richer later and when tax falls due. Hypothetically, a company worth 8,000,000 dollars freezes and grows at 7 percent. In 20 years it is worth about 30,960,000 dollars, and about 22,960,000 of that sits with the growth shares. If a system taxes accrued gains at death, using a placeholder 25 percent rate and a 500,000 dollar cost base, the founder's tax falls from about 7,615,000 dollars without a freeze to about 1,875,000 with one. That gap is mostly tax moved to another taxpayer and deferred, not saved. Meanwhile the founder's wealth stops growing, he keeps the downside, and any cash he needs comes from redemptions that may be taxed. So model his lifetime cash needs first, consider a partial freeze, and show the capped liability on his balance sheet. A licensed adviser is required before you act.
terms: Value shift — the transfer, over time, of economic value from one class of shares to another as a company grows.
Deemed disposition — a rule treating a person as having sold an asset at market value, for tax purposes, without an actual sale.
Partial freeze — a freeze applied to only part of a person's holding, leaving some future growth in their own hands.

hostile.q: Your adviser's slide says this freeze saves the family 5,700,000 dollars of tax. Is that true?
hostile.a: Not as stated. On the slide's assumptions, it moves about 5,700,000 dollars of tax liability off my estate and onto the growth shareholders, who will meet it on their own events, possibly later and possibly at different rates. Some of the value is deferral, which is real, and some depends on rules that can change. I want the adviser to show the full picture: tax moved, tax deferred and the present value of each.

title: Attribution and Deemed Disposition: Where Tax Follows You Anyway
summary: Two families of tax rules decide whether a freeze or trust works: attribution rules, which tax income or gains back to the person who transferred property, and deemed disposition rules, which treat an event such as death or the passage of time as a sale. Learn the logic of each, and how two systems might differ, before you read any statute.
body:
Tax systems expect people to try shifting income and gains to family members in lower brackets, so they contain rules that send the tax back to the person who made the transfer, and rules that create a taxable event when no sale happens. Every freeze and family trust is designed around those two families of rules.

Recall

Q. What does an estate freeze do?

A. It fixes the value of a person's current holding in fixed-value shares and lets future growth accrue to growth shares, often held by a trust.

Q. What is voidable transfer risk in concept?

A. The risk that a court sets aside a transfer made to defeat creditors, usually judged by timing, solvency and intent under local rules.

Q. Why does a lender's monitor matter to an owner?

A. It provides an independent check on work in place and cost to complete, which protects the lender and catches problems the owner's own reporting may miss.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when an adviser proposes a freeze or a family trust, the tax outcome depends less on the structure's elegance than on whether these rules bite. If you understand the logic, you can ask the one question that matters: "Which anti-shifting rules apply to this, and how does the design deal with them?" This is concept teaching. Every system writes these rules differently, and they change. Never rely on a description here as the law anywhere; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Professional sign-off required: a tax lawyer or tax accountant in each relevant jurisdiction.

Attribution in plain words

Plain English. If a parent in a high tax bracket gives investments to a young child who pays little tax, the family's total tax bill would fall. Many systems prevent that with attribution rules: rules that tax income, and sometimes gains, from property transferred to certain related people back to the person who transferred it.

The professional framing. Attribution rules usually turn on four questions. Who transferred or lent the property? To whom: a spouse, a minor child, a trust for them, a corporation they benefit from? What kind of return: interest and dividends, capital gains, or both? And on what terms: a gift, a loan at no interest, a loan at a commercial rate, or a sale at fair value? Many systems switch attribution off where the related person paid fair value or the loan carries a commercial rate that is actually paid on time. The exact categories, ages, rates and exceptions vary widely.

Applied example, hypothetical. A father lends 1,000,000 dollars interest-free to a family trust whose beneficiaries are his two children, aged 10 and 12. The trust invests and earns 50,000 dollars of dividends, which it pays out for the children. In a system with attribution rules of this kind, that 50,000 dollars may be taxed in the father's hands as if he had earned it. If instead the loan carried interest at a prescribed or commercial rate that the trust paid each year, the result might differ. The design decides the tax, and a casual design defeats the plan.

Say that out loud now.

Attribution inside a freeze

A freeze is often designed with attribution in mind. If growth shares are issued to a trust for minor children and the company pays dividends to those shares, attribution or similar rules may send the tax back to the founder in some systems. Some regimes also have special rules on income splitting through private companies that apply regardless of the classic attribution rules. The practical effect is that many freezes are designed so the trust accumulates value in the growth shares rather than receiving current income while children are young. Ask your adviser which rules apply to dividends on the growth shares, at what ages, and what the trust is permitted to do with them.

Deemed disposition in plain words

Plain English. Some systems tax a gain only when you sell. If you never sell, the gain could escape tax forever, passing down the generations untaxed. A deemed disposition rule closes that gap by treating you as having sold the asset at market value on a defined event, even though nothing was sold.

Common triggering events, in concept, include death, ceasing to be resident in a country, transferring property to a trust or a related person, and, for some trusts, the passage of a fixed number of years. A system with a periodic trust rule might, for example, treat a trust as selling its assets at regular anniversaries, so that accumulated gains inside a long-lived trust are taxed at intervals rather than never. Whether a rule like that exists, its period and its exceptions must be confirmed for each jurisdiction [unverified — confirm independently].

Second applied example, hypothetical. A trust acquires growth shares at 100 dollars. Twenty years later they are worth 20,000,000 dollars. If the governing system has a periodic deemed disposition at that point, the trust may owe tax on about 20,000,000 dollars of gain without having sold anything, and must find the cash. Trustees in such systems plan years ahead: distributing shares to beneficiaries before the date where that is permitted and sensible, arranging liquidity, or accepting the tax. A trust that ignores its own clock can be forced to sell part of a private company to pay a bill nobody planned for.

Two Systems

This is a conceptual comparison, and every point must be verified against primary source before you rely on it. Canada is commonly described as having no separate estate or inheritance tax; instead, its income tax system uses deemed dispositions, including at death and at fixed intervals for many trusts, along with attribution rules for transfers to spouses, minors and related trusts. Guyana has its own income tax and capital gains tax legislation. Whether Guyana treats death or a transfer to a trust as a disposition, whether any estate, succession or gift duty applies, how trusts are taxed, and whether attribution-style rules exist are questions to confirm against the current statutes and with a Guyanese tax adviser [unverified — confirm independently]. The lesson is not the answer for either country. It is that the same freeze can produce very different results in two systems, so each must be checked on its own terms, and a family with assets in both must have both checked together.

The questions to put to your adviser

Turn the week's rules into five questions you can read aloud in any meeting. One: which attribution or income-splitting rules could apply to this structure, and how does the design deal with each? Two: what deemed disposition events could apply to me, to the trust and to each beneficiary, and on what dates? Three: if any family member moves country, what changes? Four: what happens to cost base at each step? Five: which of these answers depends on a rule that has changed in the last few years or is under review? Ask for the answers in writing, with the rule cited, so that you, or a second adviser, can check them against the primary source. A good adviser will welcome the questions. An adviser who answers with "it's all standard" has not answered.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a structure designed for one rule set and never revisited. Anti-shifting rules are among the most frequently amended parts of tax law. The control is a written review of attribution and deemed disposition exposure at every change in law, residence, family circumstances or asset value, and a calendar showing any deemed disposition dates for each trust.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is assuming that a gift within the family moves the tax as well as the asset. Often it moves the asset and leaves the tax with the giver.

Callback

In the avoidance versus evasion week, Cole and I taught that anti-avoidance rules look at substance over form. Attribution and deemed disposition rules are the targeted, specific version of that idea: they name the shifting techniques in advance and send the tax where the system thinks it belongs.

Recap

Attribution rules send income or gains on transferred property back to the transferor; deemed disposition rules create a taxable sale without one. Both shape every freeze and trust, differ by system and change often.

Next lesson: Elias, working through a freeze's numbers step by step.
checklist: I ask which attribution rules apply to every family transfer, loan or trust.
I check whether a commercial or prescribed interest rate would switch attribution off, and whether it is actually paid.
I confirm how dividends on growth shares held for minors would be taxed.
I list every deemed disposition event that could apply: death, emigration, transfer and trust anniversaries.
I keep a calendar of any deemed disposition dates for each trust.
I plan liquidity for a deemed disposition years in advance.
I have each jurisdiction checked separately and together where assets are in both.
I review the structure whenever law, residence, family or value changes.
head: Field checklist
speak: Tax systems expect families to shift income and gains to lower-bracket relatives, so they contain two families of rules. Attribution rules tax income, and sometimes gains, from property transferred or lent to a spouse, a minor child or a trust for them back to the person who made the transfer. They often switch off where fair value was paid or a commercial interest rate is actually paid. Deemed disposition rules treat a person or a trust as having sold an asset at market value on a defined event, such as death, emigration, a transfer, or in some systems the passage of a fixed number of years for a trust. A trust that ignores its own clock can be forced to sell part of a private company to pay tax. Canada and Guyana approach these questions differently, so verify each against primary source. Review the structure whenever the law, residence, family or value changes.
terms: Attribution rules — rules that tax income or gains on property transferred to certain related people back to the transferor.
Deemed disposition — a rule treating a person or trust as having sold an asset at market value on a defined event without an actual sale.
Prescribed rate loan — a family loan carrying an interest rate set by the tax authority, used in some systems to avoid attribution if the interest is actually paid.

hostile.q: Your trust holds growth shares for your minor children and received dividends this year. Why is that income not taxable to you?
hostile.a: It may be, and I will not assert otherwise without checking. Our adviser has given us a written opinion on which attribution and income-splitting rules apply to these dividends, and how they were reported. If the opinion is that the income attributes to me, it is on my return. If it does not, the opinion sets out why, and I will provide it with the supporting trust and company records.

title: Working a Freeze Through, Step by Step
summary: A worked calculation of a hypothetical estate freeze: valuation, share exchange, growth over 15 years, the founder's tax at death with and without the freeze, and the trust's own latent gain. Every number is round and hypothetical; the method is the lesson.
body:
You understand a freeze when you can work it on one page: the value frozen, the growth that moves, the tax at death with and without the freeze, and the tax the trust now carries. Here it is, step by step.

Recall

Q. What do attribution rules do?

A. They tax income, and sometimes gains, from property transferred or lent to certain related people back to the person who made the transfer.

Q. What is position sizing in personal wealth?

A. Deciding how much of your net worth to put into any one asset or deal, so no single loss can do irreparable damage.

Q. What does a quantity surveyor's audit test?

A. Whether quantities, rates and claimed costs match the work and the contract, providing an independent check on what has been billed.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a family meeting about a freeze will be full of share diagrams. The one page of numbers is what tells you whether the plan is worth the cost and the loss of flexibility. All figures below are hypothetical round numbers. The tax rate is a placeholder, not a fact about any system; real rates, rules and exemptions must be verified against the primary source before you rely on them. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

Step one: the valuation

A founder owns 100 percent of a holding company through 1,000 ordinary shares, for which he paid 1,000 dollars, so his cost base is 1,000 dollars. A qualified business valuator values the company at 12,000,000 dollars, using the net asset value of its project interests adjusted for latent tax and a discount for lack of marketability. The valuation report records the method and evidence. The share terms will include a price adjustment clause in case the value is later challenged, where local law gives that effect.

Step two: the exchange and subscription

The founder exchanges his 1,000 ordinary shares for 12,000,000 freeze shares, each redeemable at 1 dollar, so their total redemption value is 12,000,000 dollars. They carry votes and a non-cumulative dividend right capped at a stated rate, for example 4 percent of redemption value, if declared. In many systems an exchange like this can be done without immediate tax, if the rules for a tax-deferred reorganisation are met; that is a jurisdictional question to verify. A newly settled discretionary family trust subscribes for 100 new ordinary shares at 1 dollar each, 100 dollars in total. Immediately after, the company is still worth 12,000,000 dollars, all of it attributable to the freeze shares. The growth shares are worth almost nothing.

Say that out loud now.

Step three: the growth

Assume the company grows at 6 percent a year for 15 years. One-point-oh-six raised to the 15th power is about 2.397. The company's value after 15 years is about 12,000,000 multiplied by 2.397, or about 28,760,000 dollars. The freeze shares remain worth 12,000,000 dollars, assuming no redemptions. The growth shares are worth about 16,760,000 dollars.

ItemDay oneYear 15
Company value12,000,000 dollarsabout 28,760,000 dollars
Founder's freeze shares12,000,000 dollars12,000,000 dollars
Trust's growth sharesabout 0about 16,760,000 dollars

Step four: the founder's tax at death

Suppose the founder dies in year 15 in a system that treats death as a disposition at market value, and use a placeholder effective rate of 25 percent on gains.

Without a freeze, his shares would be worth about 28,760,000 dollars. The gain would be 28,760,000 minus the 1,000 dollar cost base, effectively 28,759,000 dollars. At the placeholder rate, tax would be about 7,190,000 dollars.

With the freeze, his freeze shares are worth 12,000,000 dollars. In a tax-deferred exchange his cost base typically carries over, so it remains about 1,000 dollars. The gain is about 11,999,000 dollars, and tax is about 3,000,000 dollars.

The founder's estate tax at death falls by about 4,190,000 dollars. That figure is the one an adviser's slide will show.

Step five: what the trust now carries

The trust's growth shares, with a cost base of 100 dollars, carry a latent gain of about 16,760,000 dollars. At the same placeholder rate, that is about 4,190,000 dollars of latent tax, which is exactly the amount removed from the founder's estate. The tax has not gone. It has moved to the trust, and it will fall due on the trust's own events: a sale, a distribution that triggers tax, or, in a system with periodic trust rules, a fixed anniversary.

The value of the freeze in tax terms is therefore mostly the value of deferral. Suppose the trust's tax would otherwise fall at the founder's death in year 15, but instead falls in year 21 under a hypothetical periodic rule. Six years of deferral on 4,190,000 dollars, discounted at 5 percent, is worth roughly 4,190,000 minus 4,190,000 divided by 1.340, or about 1,060,000 dollars in present value terms. If the trust's growth shares are distributed to adult beneficiaries before any such date, where that is permitted, and the beneficiaries hold for decades, the deferral may be much longer.

Step six: test the assumptions

A second worked example, changing one input. Suppose growth is 3 percent rather than 6. After 15 years, 1.03 raised to the 15th is about 1.558, so the company is worth about 18,700,000 dollars and the growth shares about 6,700,000 dollars. The founder's tax reduction falls to about 1,675,000 dollars. Now suppose the company falls in value to 10,000,000 dollars. The freeze shares are capped at their redemption value and can be redeemed only for what the company is worth; the growth shares are worth nothing, and the freeze has moved no value at all. A freeze pays off most when growth is strong, and does nothing, while still costing fees, when it is weak. Some families respond by refreezing at a lower value after a fall; that is a design choice to check with advisers.

Step seven: the cost of doing it

A freeze is not free, and the benefit must be compared with the cost. Hypothetically, suppose the valuation costs 25,000 dollars, legal and tax advice on the reorganisation and the trust costs 60,000 dollars, and the trust's annual administration and filings cost 15,000 dollars a year. Over 15 years, at a 5 percent discount rate, the present value of 15,000 dollars a year is about 15,000 multiplied by 10.38, or about 155,700 dollars. Add the upfront 85,000 dollars and the total cost in present value is about 240,700 dollars. On the 6 percent growth case, the deferral alone was worth about 1,060,000 dollars, comfortably more. On a low-growth case, the benefit can fall close to the cost. That is why the low case belongs on the summary page, and why a family should freeze when the expected growth is large enough to carry the cost with room to spare.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is showing the family only the founder's tax saving at death, without the trust's matching latent tax and its own clock. The control is a one-page summary with all four lines: value frozen, value shifted, tax moved off the estate, and latent tax now in the trust with its likely date.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is forgetting the cost base. A freeze that resets cost base, or fails to carry it over, can create tax on day one. Ask exactly what happens to cost base at every step.

Callback

In the returns week, Sage taught that an after-tax return must count every leakage and every timing difference. A freeze is a pure timing-and-taxpayer move, so value it the same way: in present value, after every tax, for every party.

Recap

Value, exchange, grow, compare the estate's tax with and without the freeze, then show the trust's latent tax and its clock. Test growth and decline. The freeze moves tax and buys deferral; it does not delete tax.

Next lesson: Elias, in the room with a founder who wants to freeze and keep every dividend.
checklist: I start every freeze analysis with an independent valuation and the cost base.
I confirm whether the share exchange can be done without immediate tax locally.
I project company value at the stated growth rate and at a low and negative case.
I compute the founder's tax at death with and without the freeze.
I show the trust's matching latent tax and when it may fall due.
I value the deferral in present value terms.
I check what happens to cost base at every step.
I present all four lines on one page to the family.
head: Field checklist
speak: Here is a freeze on one page, with hypothetical numbers and a placeholder 25 percent tax rate. A founder's company is valued independently at 12,000,000 dollars; his cost base is 1,000 dollars. He exchanges his shares for freeze shares redeemable at 12,000,000, and a family trust subscribes for growth shares at 100 dollars. At 6 percent growth for 15 years, the company reaches about 28,760,000 dollars, and the trust's shares hold about 16,760,000. If death is taxed as a disposition, the founder's tax falls from about 7,190,000 dollars without the freeze to about 3,000,000 with it. But the trust now carries a matching latent tax of about 4,190,000 dollars on its own clock. So the freeze moves tax and buys deferral. At 3 percent growth the benefit shrinks; if value falls, it moves nothing. Always show all four lines, and verify every rule against the primary source.
terms: Cost base — the amount treated as paid for an asset for tax purposes, from which gain is measured.
Tax-deferred reorganisation — a share exchange that some systems allow without immediate tax if defined conditions are met.
Refreeze — a later reorganisation that resets the frozen value, often after a fall in the company's value.

hostile.q: Your model shows 4,190,000 dollars of tax saving. Where does that money go?
hostile.a: It does not disappear. It moves from my estate to the trust as a latent tax on the growth shares, of the same amount on these assumptions. What we gain is a change of taxpayer and deferral, which I have valued at about 1,060,000 dollars in present value on a six-year delay at 5 percent. The model also shows that at 3 percent growth the effect is much smaller, and that if the company falls in value, the freeze moves nothing.

title: The Founder Who Wants to Freeze and Keep Every Dividend
summary: A hypothetical founder wants an estate freeze, full control, every future dividend, and the tax benefit too. The scene shows how to hear the real worry behind the request, the lines that keep the conversation honest, the lines never to say, and when silence does the work.
body:
The founder who wants to freeze his company and keep every dividend is not asking for a tax structure. He is asking whether he can give the future to his children without becoming dependent on them, and that question has an answer he can live with.

Recall

Q. In a freeze, what does the trust's latent gain represent?

A. The tax moved off the founder's estate onto the growth shares, which falls due on the trust's own events rather than disappearing.

Q. What is the main argument for keeping a liquidity floor?

A. So that obligations can be met without forced sales or borrowing at bad terms when markets or circumstances turn.

Q. What does an independent peer review add to a design?

A. A second qualified opinion from someone with no stake in the original work, which catches errors and assumptions the designer cannot see.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will sit in rooms like this as the founder, as an adviser's client, or as a partner whose co-owner is planning his estate. The tax concepts from this week only matter if the people in the room make honest decisions. This scene is hypothetical. The people and numbers are invented for teaching.

The scene

A hypothetical developer in his sixties, whom we will call Mr Grant, owns a holding company worth 15,000,000 dollars. He has three adult children and two grandchildren. His accountant has proposed a freeze with growth shares going to a discretionary family trust. Mr Grant opens the meeting: "I like it. But I want to keep voting control, I want all the dividends to keep coming to me, I want to be able to unwind it if one of the kids goes off the rails, and I want the tax saving. Make that work."

The question behind the question

The real question is fear of dependence. He has run his own life on his own cash for 40 years. A freeze feels like handing his future to children who might divorce, quarrel or disappoint him. The request for "all the dividends" and "the right to unwind" is a request for safety, not for tax. The useful conversation addresses safety directly.

The lines to say

Begin by naming the trade honestly: "Each of those four goals is reasonable. Some of them pull against the others. A freeze works because the future really does leave your hands. The more of it you keep, the less it does."

Then turn the fear into numbers: "Before we design anything, let us work out what you need. How much a year do you want to live on, for how long, and what would you want in reserve for a bad decade? If your freeze shares and your other assets cover that with room to spare, we freeze only what is above it."

On control: "Voting control is often possible through the terms of your freeze shares, subject to the rules here. That keeps you running the company."

On dividends: "You can receive dividends on your freeze shares within their terms. Dividends on the growth shares belong to the trust, and if they go to young beneficiaries, attribution or similar rules may send the tax back to you. We would design around that, not ignore it."

On unwinding: "The trust can be discretionary, with a family trustee and an independent trustee, so no child receives anything by right. A protector can be named. That gives you a voice through the structure without making it your own pocket, which would risk the whole thing being treated as yours."

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

Never say "Don't worry, the trust is really yours." That sentence invites the very sham and control problems that undo trusts, and it will be quoted.

Never say "This saves you 4,000,000 dollars." On this week's numbers, most of that figure is tax moved and deferred. Say "it moves about that much liability off your estate and defers it".

Never promise an unwind. Once growth value sits in the trust, taking it back can be costly or impossible, and a structure designed to be easily reversed may not achieve the result at all.

When to stay silent

Stay silent after you ask how much he needs to feel safe. Founders rarely say that number aloud, and the silence is often where they find it. Stay silent, too, when he says "So you are telling me I can't have it all." Let him reach the conclusion himself. A decision he owns will survive the first family argument; one he was talked into will not.

A worked example in the room

Hypothetically, Mr Grant says he wants 400,000 dollars a year after tax for 25 years, rising with inflation, plus a 2,000,000 dollar reserve. Using the method from last week's numbers lesson, assume a real after-tax return on his personal assets of 2 percent. The present value of 400,000 dollars a year for 25 years at 2 percent is about 400,000 multiplied by 19.52, or about 7,810,000 dollars. Add the reserve and he needs about 9,810,000 dollars of value under his own control. If he has 2,000,000 dollars outside the company, he needs about 7,810,000 dollars from the freeze shares. That points to a partial freeze, or a full freeze at 15,000,000 dollars with a planned schedule of redemptions to fund his life, each of which has its own tax cost to model. Either way, the conversation is now about his life, not a diagram.

Holding your state

Founders in this room are often angry at their own mortality, and that anger can land on the adviser. Notice it, do not argue with it, and keep your voice level and slow. Your value is that you are not afraid of him and not selling him anything.

Ending the meeting well

Close the meeting with three written items, not a handshake. First, a one-page note of Mr Grant's stated needs: the income, the reserve, the control he wants and the outcomes he fears. Second, a list of the decisions still open: full or partial freeze, who the trustees are, whether to name a protector, and what the dividend policy will be. Third, the next steps, with names and dates: the valuator's engagement, the lawyer's first draft, the accountant's tax memo. Send the note the same day and ask him to correct anything that does not match what he meant. A founder who sees his own fears written down calmly is far more likely to make a steady decision than one who leaves with an impression. It is also the record that protects every adviser in the room if a child later says the founder was pressured.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is designing to the founder's first sentence instead of his underlying need, producing a structure that keeps so much control it fails, or gives away so much he resents it. The control is a written statement of his needs and goals, agreed before design, and a design memo that shows how each goal is met or why it is traded off.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is answering the tax question first. Answer the life question first, then size the freeze to it. Professional sign-off required: a tax lawyer or tax accountant, and a trust lawyer, in the relevant jurisdiction.

Callback

In the wealth mindset week, Warrick asked you to define "enough" for yourself. Mr Grant's reserve and income are his version of enough. A freeze sized above that figure is generosity; one sized below it is fear waiting to happen.

Recap

Name the trade, turn fear into a number, keep control through share terms, design dividends around attribution, use a discretionary trust with independence, never promise an unwind, and let the founder reach the decision.

Next lesson: Kema, with six questions and drills on freezes, attribution and deemed disposition.
checklist: I name the trade-offs between control, income, reversibility and tax at the start.
I ask the founder what he needs to feel safe, in dollars, before designing.
I size the freeze to his lifetime needs and reserve.
I keep control through share terms, not by treating the trust as his.
I design dividend flows around attribution rules.
I never promise that a freeze can be unwound.
I present tax effects as moved and deferred.
I write the agreed needs and goals down before any design work.
head: Field checklist
speak: A hypothetical founder wants an estate freeze, voting control, every dividend, the right to unwind and the tax saving. His real question is fear of dependence on his children. So name the trade: a freeze works because the future really leaves your hands, and the more you keep, the less it does. Then turn the fear into a number. If he wants 400,000 dollars a year for 25 years at a 2 percent real return plus a 2,000,000 dollar reserve, he needs about 9,810,000 dollars under his own control, which points to a partial freeze or planned redemptions. Control can come through share terms. Dividends to young beneficiaries may attribute back. A discretionary trust with an independent trustee and a protector gives him a voice without making it his pocket. Never say the trust is really his, never call moved tax saved, never promise an unwind, and stay silent while he finds his number.
terms: Protector — a person named in some trust deeds with power to approve or veto key trustee decisions.
Redemption schedule — a planned sequence of redeeming freeze shares to fund the founder's income, each with its own tax cost.
Sham — an arrangement whose documents do not reflect what the parties genuinely intended, which a court may disregard.

hostile.q: If I sign this freeze and my son divorces, does his wife get a share of the company?
hostile.a: I cannot give you a legal answer, and your lawyer must. What I can say is that the design matters. If growth shares go to a discretionary trust rather than to your son directly, he has no fixed share, only a hope, which in many systems makes his interest harder to treat as his property. The outcome still depends on local family and trust law, the deed and the facts, so we will get that advice before you sign, not after.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 91 Review: Freezes, Attribution and the Trust's Own Clock
summary: Six questions test the estate freeze, Fundy Settlement, value shift, attribution and deemed disposition. A Red Pen drill finds the defects in a hypothetical freeze memo. A boardroom drill explains a freeze in two minutes.
body:
This week came down to one idea: a freeze and a family trust move value and tax to other people and other dates, and every rule this week exists to check whether that move is real.

Recall

Q. What is the most useful first question to ask a founder planning a freeze?

A. How much he needs, in dollars, to feel safe for the rest of his life, so the freeze can be sized above that figure.

Q. What is Rule 90?

A. Never let a trustee deal with trust property for his own benefit or with a connected party unless the deed allows it, beneficiaries or the court consent in writing, and the decision and price are documented independently.

Q. Why are independent reviews valuable to an owner?

A. Because people with no stake in the result catch optimism, errors and conflicts that the owner's own team will not.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six questions without notes, you can judge a freeze proposal and ask an adviser the questions that matter. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What does an estate freeze move, and what does it leave behind?

Answer: It moves future growth from the founder's shares to growth shares, often held by a trust. It leaves the founder with today's value, any existing latent gain on it, and usually the first loss if value falls.

Question 2. Why does a freeze need an independent valuation and often a price adjustment clause?

Answer: Because a wrong frozen value either makes an unintended taxable gift or loads the freeze shares with value the company cannot support, and a price adjustment clause, where effective, corrects the redemption amount if the value is challenged.

Question 3. State Rule 91 and the case behind it.

Answer: Never rest a structure's tax result on an address; it lives where real decisions are made, so make them there and keep the evidence. Fundy Settlement, Supreme Court of Canada, 2012: trusts with a Barbados trustee were held resident in Canada, where central management and control was exercised.

Question 4. What do attribution rules do?

Answer: They tax income, and sometimes gains, from property transferred or lent to certain related people back to the transferor, often switching off where fair value or a commercial rate is actually paid.

Question 5. What is a deemed disposition, and name three possible triggers.

Answer: A rule treating a person or trust as having sold an asset at market value without a sale. Possible triggers include death, ceasing to be resident, transfer to a trust or related person, and, in some systems, a trust's fixed anniversary.

Question 6. Why is the founder's tax saving at death not money saved?

Answer: Because a matching latent tax moves onto the growth shares and falls due on the trust's own events. The real benefit is a change of taxpayer and deferral, which should be valued in present value terms.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Tessa and Elias framed the freeze: fixed-value shares for today, growth shares for tomorrow. Ford and Cole took Fundy Settlement through seven steps and gave Rule 91. Warrick measured value shift and its effect on the founder's balance sheet. Elias taught attribution, deemed disposition and two systems compared. Elias worked a freeze through, step by step. Elias ran the room with a founder who wanted to keep everything.

Red Pen

Read this hypothetical adviser's memo and find the defects before reading on.

Memo to Mr Founder. Recommendation: freeze your holding company at 9,000,000 dollars, being our estimate of value. Growth shares will be issued to a trust for your children, aged 8 and 11, which will receive annual dividends of about 300,000 dollars to fund their schooling, taxed at their low rates. You will remain sole trustee so the trust stays under your control. The trustee will be a company in a low-tax country to keep the trust offshore. The freeze saves 3,500,000 dollars of tax permanently. It can be reversed at any time if needed.

The defects. First, the frozen value is "our estimate", not an independent valuation, and there is no price adjustment clause. Second, dividends to a trust for minor children may be attributed back to the founder or caught by income-splitting rules; "taxed at their low rates" is an assumption, not a conclusion. Third, the founder as sole trustee keeping control contradicts the next sentence about an offshore corporate trustee; the memo names two different trustees. Fourth, if the founder controls the trust, Rule 91 says its residence may follow him, so the offshore trustee would not move it. Fifth, sole control by the settlor also raises sham and control risk. Sixth, the tax is not saved permanently; it moves to the growth shares and is deferred. Seventh, a freeze generally cannot be reversed at will without cost, and a reversible design may fail to achieve its purpose.

Common confusions

Four confusions recur this week. First, "a freeze makes tax disappear". It moves the latent tax to the growth shares and defers it. Second, "the trustee is offshore, so the trust is offshore". Rule 91 says the trust lives where real decisions are made. Third, "I gave it to my children, so the income is theirs". Attribution rules in some systems send income on transferred property back to the giver. Fourth, "the trust can hold the shares forever". Some systems impose a periodic deemed disposition on trusts, and many limit how long a trust can last, so a trust needs a calendar. If you hear any of these sentences in a meeting, slow the conversation down and ask for the rule, in writing, with the source.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a family adopting a freeze on a slide that shows only the estate's saving. The control is the one-page, four-line summary: value frozen, value shifted, tax moved and latent tax in the trust with its date.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is thinking a freeze is a tax product. It is a family decision with tax consequences, and the family decision comes first.

Boardroom drill

Explain an estate freeze in two minutes to a family council that includes adult children who are not in the business. Then read the model answer.

Model answer: "Today the company is worth about 12,000,000 dollars, all of it in my name. If nothing changes, every dollar of future growth stays with me until I die, when tax and probate may arrive together. A freeze fixes my stake at 12,000,000 dollars in shares that keep my vote but stop growing. New shares, which will hold all future growth, go to a discretionary trust for the family, with an independent trustee alongside a family trustee. Nobody receives anything by right, and the trustees decide according to written wishes and their duties. The tax does not disappear; it moves to the trust and is deferred, and the trust has its own rules and dates we will plan for. I am freezing only what I do not need to live on. You will each receive the deed, my letter of wishes and a one-page summary of the numbers."

Callback

In the post-mortem on partnerships, we saw related-party dealing hide behind good intentions. A founder who is sole trustee of a trust holding his own company's growth shares is a related-party structure by design. Independence is not decoration; it is what makes the freeze his family's rather than his.

Recap

A freeze moves growth and latent tax to growth shares, needs a real valuation, real trustees and real decisions, meets attribution and deemed disposition rules, and is sized to the founder's own needs.

head: The six questions
speak: This week: estate freezes and the tax rules around them. A freeze exchanges a founder's shares for fixed-value freeze shares, so future growth goes to growth shares, often held by a discretionary trust. It needs an independent valuation and often a price adjustment clause. Fundy Settlement, decided by the Supreme Court of Canada in 2012, held that trusts with a Barbados trustee were resident in Canada because central management and control was exercised there, which gave Rule 91: a structure lives where real decisions are made. Attribution rules can send income on transferred property back to the transferor, and deemed disposition rules can tax a gain at death, emigration, transfer or a trust's anniversary without a sale. The founder's tax saving at death is mostly tax moved and deferred, matched by latent tax in the trust. Size the freeze to the founder's own needs first. Verify every rule against the primary source.
terms: Growth shares — ordinary shares issued in a freeze that carry all value above the frozen amount.
Income splitting — shifting income to lower-taxed family members, which attribution and related rules often restrict.
Latent tax — tax that would fall due if an asset were sold or deemed sold at its current value.

hostile.q: You are a trustee of the trust that holds your company's growth shares. How is that trust independent of you?
hostile.a: On its own, it would not be, which is why I am not the only trustee. The deed appoints an independent professional trustee with me, both must agree every decision, I declare my interest and step out of any decision about my own company, and the minutes record it. The trustees take their own advice. If you think that is not enough, I would rather discuss stepping down as trustee than leave you in doubt.
